faq-u3-a1.title: Library and user-defined functions
paragraphs: A function is a named block of statements that performs a specific task. Functions are of two types:
faq-u3-a1.authority: PankusDesk-authored exam answer based on the ingested notes

items.label: Library functions
items.text: Predefined functions provided by the C library, such as printf(), scanf() and strlen(). Include the appropriate header before using them.

items.label: User-defined functions
items.text: Functions written by the programmer to perform a required task, such as adding two numbers.

blocks.label: Example of a user-defined function

faq-u3-a2.title: Actual and formal parameters
paragraphs: Actual arguments and formal parameters are distinguished as follows:
faq-u3-a2.authority: PankusDesk-authored exam answer based on the ingested notes

rows: Expressions supplied in a function call.
Variables declared in the function definition.
Their values are passed to the called function.
They receive copies of the argument values.
In add(x, y), x and y are actual arguments.
In int add(int a, int b), a and b are formal parameters.

faq-u3-a3.title: Function syntax
paragraphs: A user-defined function is used through its declaration, call and definition.
faq-u3-a3.authority: PankusDesk-authored exam answer based on the ingested notes

blocks.text: The declaration tells the compiler the function name, return type and parameter types.

blocks.code: int add(int, int);

blocks.text: The call executes the function. Here 5 and 3 are the actual arguments, and the returned value is assigned to total.

blocks.code: int total = add(5, 3);

blocks.text: The definition contains the statements that perform the task. int is the return type; add is the name; a and b are formal parameters; return sends the result back to the caller.

faq-u3-a4.title: Recursion and its characteristics
paragraphs: Recursion is the process in which a function calls itself to solve a smaller instance of a problem.
faq-u3-a4.authority: PankusDesk-authored exam answer based on the ingested notes
faq-u3-a4.basis_label: Priyanka class notes, supplemented by senior notes

items.label: Base case
items.text: Stops further recursive calls.

items.label: Recursive case
items.text: Calls the function with an argument closer to the base case.

blocks.label: Example: factorial for small nonnegative inputs

faq-u3-a5.title: Functions and modular programming
paragraphs: The advantages of functions are:
faq-u3-a5.authority: PankusDesk-authored exam answer based on the ingested notes

items.label: Reusability
items.text: A function can be called multiple times, avoiding repeated code.

items.label: Reduced complexity
items.text: A large problem can be divided into smaller, manageable tasks.

items.label: Readability
items.text: Each function performs a specific task, making the program easier to understand.

items.label: Easy testing and debugging
items.text: Functions can be tested separately, helping locate errors.

items.label: Easy maintenance
items.text: A function can be modified without rewriting the entire program.

faq-u3-a5.research_note: The five-point exam answer expands the ingested functions/task organization material; it is authored synthesis, not a verbatim list in Priyanka images 70–72.

faq-u3-a6.title: Library and user-defined functions
paragraphs: Four commonly used C library functions are:
faq-u3-a6.authority: PankusDesk-authored exam answer based on the ingested notes

rows: Finds the length of a string, excluding its null terminator.

blocks.text: Library functions provide ready-made operations, reducing the code the programmer must write.

faq-u3-a7.title: Storage classes
paragraphs: For an ordinary local variable declared inside a block, the default storage class is auto.
faq-u3-a7.authority: PankusDesk-authored exam answer based on the ingested notes

blocks.text: register suggests fast access to the compiler. In C11, applying the address-of operator (&) to a register variable is not allowed, so an expression such as &b causes a compilation diagnostic.

faq-u3-q1.title: Functions and modular programming
paragraphs: A function is a named block that performs a particular task. Its declaration, call and definition are:
faq-u3-q1.authority: PankusDesk-authored exam answer based on the ingested notes

items.label: Declaration
items.text: Introduces the return type, name and parameter types before the function is called: static void fact(unsigned);

items.label: Call
items.text: Transfers control to the function: fact(n);. n is the actual argument.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Provides the function body: static void fact(unsigned m) { ... }. m is the formal parameter.

blocks.text: A prototype describes the function’s interface: its return type and parameter types. Structured programming divides a larger task into functions with clear responsibilities.
In the factorial example, the accumulator starts at 1 and is multiplied by each integer from 1 through m. For m = 5, the products are 1, 2, 6, 24 and 120.

faq-u3-q2.title: Four function interfaces
paragraphs: Functions are classified into four categories according to whether they take arguments and return a value.
faq-u3-q2.authority: PankusDesk-authored exam answer based on the ingested notes

blocks.text: The caller supplies the values, and the function prints the result. Its return type is void.

blocks.code: void sum_print(int a, int b);

blocks.text: The function reads the values and prints their sum. It takes no arguments and returns no value.

blocks.code: void sum_read_print(void);

blocks.text: The caller supplies the values, and the function returns their sum for the caller to use.

blocks.code: int sum_value(int a, int b);

blocks.text: The function reads the values internally and returns their sum.

blocks.code: int sum_read_value(void);

faq-u3-q3.title: Value and address arguments
paragraphs: C passes arguments by value. Passing an address allows a function to change the caller’s object; this technique is commonly called “call by reference” in introductory C.
faq-u3-q3.authority: PankusDesk-authored exam answer based on the ingested notes

rows: Copies an ordinary value into a parameter.
Copies an address into a pointer parameter.
Changing the parameter does not change the original variable.
Writing through *x or *y changes the original variable.

blocks.text: For a = 2 and b = 3, swapping local copies x and y leaves the caller’s a and b unchanged: 2 and 3.
Pass &a and &b. Save *x, assign *x = *y, then assign *y = saved. The original a and b become 3 and 2.

faq-u3-q3.final_answer: Result: value swapping leaves the caller as 2, 3; pointer swapping changes it to 3, 2.

faq-u3-q4.title: Recursive factorial
paragraphs: Recursion is a function calling itself. The factorial of a nonnegative integer is defined by:
faq-u3-q4.authority: PankusDesk-authored exam answer based on the ingested notes
faq-u3-q4.basis_label: Priyanka class notes, supplemented by senior notes

items.text: fact(0) = 1 — the base case.
fact(n) = n × fact(n − 1), for n > 0 — the recursive case.

blocks.text: Each call decreases n by 1. When the base case returns 1, the waiting calls multiply their results.

faq-u3-q5.title: Factorial, GCD, Ackermann and Fibonacci
paragraphs: The Fibonacci series begins with 0 and 1. Each subsequent term is the sum of the previous two terms.
faq-u3-q5.authority: PankusDesk-authored exam answer based on the ingested notes

items.text: fib(0) = 0 and fib(1) = 1 are the base cases.
For n ≥ 2, fib(n) = fib(n − 1) + fib(n − 2).
To print n terms, call fib(i) for i = 0 through n − 1.

blocks.text: For example, fib(4) = fib(3) + fib(2) = 2 + 1 = 3. The program uses direct recursion and limits the term count to keep the example quick to run.

faq-u3-q6.title: Factorial, GCD, Ackermann and Fibonacci
paragraphs: To find the sum of the first n natural numbers recursively, add n to the sum of the first n − 1 numbers.
faq-u3-q6.authority: PankusDesk-authored exam answer based on the ingested notes

items.text: sum(0) = 0 is the base case.
sum(n) = n + sum(n − 1), for n > 0, is the recursive case.

blocks.text: For n = 10: sum(10) = 10 + sum(9) = 10 + 9 + sum(8) = … = 10 + 9 + … + 1 + sum(0). As the calls return, the partial sums are 0, 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, 28, 36, 45 and 55.

faq-u3-q7.title: Ackermann function
paragraphs: The Ackermann function is a recursive function defined for nonnegative integers m and n. It uses the following three cases:
faq-u3-q7.authority: PankusDesk-authored exam answer based on the ingested notes

blocks.text: The inner recursive result becomes the second argument of the outer call.

faq-u3-q8.title: Storage classes
paragraphs: Storage classes describe how variables are declared and used, including their scope and storage duration. The four classes commonly studied are auto, register, static and extern.
faq-u3-q8.authority: PankusDesk-authored exam answer based on the ingested notes

rows: For the execution of that block.
Local; suggests fast access. Its address cannot be taken in C11.
For the execution of that block.
Name is local, but its value is retained between calls.
Declares an object commonly defined at file scope or in another file.
The referenced file-scope object exists throughout execution.
An extern declaration does not initialize it; an uninitialized file-scope definition is zero-initialized.

items.label: auto
items.text: auto int a = 2; declares an automatic local variable.

items.label: register
items.text: register int count = 0; requests fast access without guaranteeing a CPU register.

items.label: static
items.text: static int calls; retains its value across function calls.

items.label: extern
items.text: extern int shared; refers to an object defined elsewhere, for example int shared = 20; at file scope.

faq-u3-q9.title: Local/global variables and lifetime
paragraphs: Scope is the region of a program where a variable’s name can be used. Lifetime is the period during which its object exists.
faq-u3-q9.authority: PankusDesk-authored exam answer based on the ingested notes

rows: From its declaration to the end of its source file, unless hidden by another declaration.

items.label: Block scope
items.text: An inner variable can hide an outer variable with the same name. Printing outer a = 2, inner a = 20, then outer a again gives 2, 20, 2.

items.label: Static lifetime
items.text: A local static counter begins at zero and retains its value. Three calls that print then increment it give 0, 1, 2.

faq-u3-q10.title: Pass arrays to functions
paragraphs: Array data can be passed to a function as individual elements or through an array parameter.
faq-u3-q10.authority: PankusDesk-authored exam answer based on the ingested notes

blocks.text: Pass selected values, such as add(a[0], a[1]). The parameters receive copies of those elements; modifying them does not modify the original array.

blocks.code: int add(int x, int y) { return x + y; }

blocks.text: Pass the array name and its length, such as lin(a, n, target). The array expression supplies a pointer to its first element. The function can access the elements through that pointer; it must receive the length separately.

blocks.code: int lin(const int a[], int n, int target);

blocks.text: The examples below add two individual elements and search an array for a target. In linear search, compare each element with the target; return 1 on a match and 0 if no element matches.

faq-u3-q10.research_note: The main scalar example uses the compilation’s first two elements. Priyanka’s separate source variant selects the third and fifth elements; those indices are not claimed for this example.

faq-u3-q11.title: Library and user-defined functions
paragraphs: C library functions are predefined operations supplied by the implementation. Include the header that declares a function before calling it.
faq-u3-q11.authority: PankusDesk-authored exam answer based on the ingested notes

rows: Counts characters before the null terminator.
Copies a string into a destination.
Compares strings; result is negative, zero or positive.

blocks.text: For strcpy and strcat, the destination must have enough space for the characters and the terminating null character. strcat adds no space automatically.

faq-u4-a2.title: Pointers and their uses
paragraphs: A pointer is a variable that stores an address. Its declaration specifies the type of object it points to.
faq-u4-a2.authority: PankusDesk-authored exam answer based on the ingested notes

faq-u4-a3.title: Structures, tags and member access
paragraphs: The arrow operator (->) accesses a structure or union member through a pointer.

faq-u4-a4.title: Structures versus unions
paragraphs: A union has the following advantage and disadvantage:
faq-u4-a4.authority: PankusDesk-authored exam answer based on the ingested notes

items.label: Advantage — memory saving
items.text: Its members share storage, so it is useful when only one of several alternative values is needed at a time.

items.label: Disadvantage — values are not retained independently
items.text: Writing one member overwrites the shared storage. A union cannot be used like a structure to preserve all member values simultaneously.

faq-u4-q1.title: Structures, tags and member access
paragraphs: A structure groups related data into a single record. A student record can contain an integer roll number, a character-array name and floating-point marks.

blocks.label: Structure definition

items.text: Declare a structure variable or an array of structure variables.
Read each member using the dot operator, such as s[i].roll_no.
Use & for numeric scanf destinations; pass the name array directly with a bounded %19s conversion.
Display each student’s members using the dot operator.

faq-u4-q2.title: Structures versus unions
paragraphs: Structures and unions both group named members, but their memory allocation differs.
faq-u4-q2.authority: PankusDesk-authored exam answer based on the ingested notes

rows: All members can hold values simultaneously.
Members do not retain independent values simultaneously.
Includes member storage and possible padding.
Enough for the largest member, with possible padding.
Records needing all fields, such as a student’s name and marks.
Alternative values, such as either an integer or a float.

blocks.text: In the union program, read and print the roll number before storing marks, then print marks before storing the name. Each new member value uses the same shared storage. Use sizeof to find the actual size on a particular implementation.

faq-u4-q3.title: Arrays and structures
paragraphs: An array of structures stores several records of the same structure type. For example, struct student s[100]; can store up to 100 student records.
faq-u4-q3.authority: PankusDesk-authored exam answer based on the ingested notes

blocks.text: Here s[i] is one student, while s[i].marks[j] is that student’s mark in subject j. Thus the example uses both an array of structures and an array within each structure.

items.text: Read the number of students n and the number of subjects m.
For each student, read the roll number, name and m marks.
Reset sum to zero for each student, then add that student’s marks.
Compute average = sum / m using floating-point division and print the average.

faq-u4-q4.title: Nested structures
paragraphs: A nested structure is a structure that contains another structure as a member.
faq-u4-q4.authority: PankusDesk-authored exam answer based on the ingested notes

items.text: Define the inner structure, such as a birthday containing month, day and year.
Include an object of that type as a member of the outer student structure.
Use consecutive dot operators to access an inner member, for example s.birth.day.

faq-u4-q5.title: Passing structures to functions
paragraphs: A pointer to a structure stores the address of a structure object. Access its members using the arrow operator (->).
faq-u4-q5.authority: PankusDesk-authored exam answer based on the ingested notes

blocks.label: Declaration and initialization

items.text: Define the structure and create an object.
Store the object’s address in a compatible structure pointer.
Use pointer->member to read or modify a member.

faq-u4-q6.title: Passing structures to functions
paragraphs: Structures can be passed to functions by value or by passing their address.
faq-u4-q6.authority: PankusDesk-authored exam answer based on the ingested notes

blocks.text: The function receives a copy of the structure. Changing that copy does not change the caller’s object. A function may also return a structure.

blocks.code: Complex add(Complex a, Complex b);

blocks.text: For complex-number addition, add the real parts and the imaginary parts separately: (1.5 + 2i) + (3 + 4.5i) = 4.5 + 6.5i.
The function receives a pointer to the original structure and accesses members with ->. A writable pointer permits changes to the original; a const pointer can be used for read-only access.

/* Call: display(&student_object); */

blocks.text: This is commonly taught as “call by reference”; the pointer value itself is still passed by value.

faq-u4-q7.title: Pointers and their uses

faq-extra-2.title: Pointer arithmetic and pointers to arrays
paragraphs: An array is a collection of elements of the same type. A pointer is a separate object that stores an address.
faq-extra-2.authority: PankusDesk-authored exam answer based on the ingested notes

rows: int a[3] allocates three int elements.
The array object cannot be reassigned to another array.
p can be assigned another compatible address.
sizeof a gives the whole array size in its defining scope.
sizeof p gives the pointer object’s size.

blocks.text: In most expressions, a converts to a pointer to its first element. For a valid index i, *(a + i) and a[i] refer to the same element. Advancing an int pointer by 1 moves to the next int element.

items.text: Read each element using scanf("%d", p), where p points to that element.

paragraphs: sizeof gives the size of a structure in bytes, including any padding inserted for alignment. Its result has type size_t.
